title: A hymn in Gujri
hook: a crane flies far from her chicks; who feeds them?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Raga Gujri, and your line was quiet devotion. Did you manage one kind thing without mentioning it? Don't tell anyone now either. Day one thousand seventy-five.

A crane lifts off from a marsh and flies a long way, leaving her chicks behind in the reeds. Who feeds them while she's gone? Who teaches them anything? That question isn't from a nature program. It's from a hymn of Guru Arjan in Raga Gujri, and it's one that a Sikh praying the evening Rehras says aloud. Which is a small surprise: yesterday's raga belongs to the morning, yet some of its hymns are carried into the evening prayer. Today: a hymn in Gujri.
screen: `A CRANE FLIES FAR.` → `WHO FEEDS THE CHICKS?` → `A GUJRI HYMN AT EVENING.`

segments.voice: The hymn opens by talking to the mind, given here in plain English: why, mind, do you keep scheming and straining, when the Lord himself is already busy with your care? Then the pictures come. In rocks and stones the Creator places living things, and sets their food in front of them. Then the crane. She flies far away, her chicks are left behind, and no one is there to feed them or teach them to peck. Think about it in your mind, the hymn says. Who looks after them? Guru Arjan isn't telling anyone to stop working. Sikh teaching prizes honest labor. The target is the anxious part of the mind that plans every outcome as if everything rested on it, the mind that's still running the numbers at two in the morning. Against that, the hymn sets a slower kind of trust: you do your part, and the care was there before you started. Now, the same raga holds a very different voice. Bhagat Trilochan, one of the saints whose words the Gurus gathered into the Granth, asks a sharper question in Gujri: at the very end, what fills the mind? Thoughts of wealth, of wife and sons, of a fine mansion, each one shapes what comes next, he says, and only the one who remembers the Lord goes free. Two voices, one raga. One soothes an anxious mind; one wakes a distracted one. Both bring the mind back to the same place. That's the devotion Gujri carries: steady, unshowy, pointed at what matters. Today's line: devotion in gujri.
screen: `WHY SCHEME AND STRAIN, MIND?` · `FOOD SET OUT IN THE ROCKS.` · `WHO FEEDS THE CRANE'S CHICKS?` · `TRILOCHAN: WHAT FILLS THE MIND AT THE END?` · then, large: `DEVOTION IN GUJRI.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: set one worry down for the length of the bell. Sit, and breathe out longer than you breathe in. Find the plan your mind keeps rehearsing today, the email, the bill, the conversation. Picture it as something you're carrying, and set it on the floor beside you. It'll still be there after. For now, picture the crane's chicks in the reeds, fed by no effort of their own. If you pray, you can say Waheguru and let the worry rest there. If you don't, let your hands lie open. This evening, listen to one Gujri shabad. The bell holds the time.
A hymn in Gujri. Guru Arjan's crane, flying far while her chicks are cared for, and Bhagat Trilochan asking what fills the mind at the end. Today's word.
Your line: devotion in gujri. The next time you catch your mind scheming, ask it the hymn's question, why, mind?, and take one slow breath before answering. Day one thousand seventy-five.

howItsDone: Guru Arjan's Gujri hymn about the anxious mind and the crane is part of the Rehras, the evening prayer Sikhs recite or sing at sunset; in kirtan it is sung in Raga Gujri.

fork.setup: the crane has flown far, and her chicks are alone in the reeds. who looks after them, by the hymn's account?
options: nobody, so they must fend for themselves.
the Lord, who cares for every creature.
the other cranes of the flock.
fork.reveal: the hymn asks the mind to think about it: the same Creator who sets food before creatures in the rocks cares for the chicks too.

trapdoor: what you thought: a hymn in gujri is just a song in a certain key.
what it means: a hymn that turns a scheming mind toward trust, with a crane and her chicks as the picture.
what a scholar hears: Guru Arjan's Gujri shabad also stands in the Rehras, and beside it in the raga stands Bhagat Trilochan's verse on what the mind holds at the end.

sources.ref: Gujri, Mahala 5, Ang 495; also in the Rehras, Ang 10

notes: Guru Arjan's 'kahe re man chitvahi udam' (Gujri M5, Ang 495; Rehras Ang 10) is paraphrased: the mind's scheming, creatures in rocks and stones given their food, the crane (kunj) flying far leaving its young unfed and untaught. The text names a distance (sai kosa) that was left out of the voice. Please confirm.
The outline mentions 'the evening Rehras hymns'; only Guru Arjan's Gujri hymn is named. Guru Ram Das's 'har ke jan satgur satpurkha' (also Gujri, in the Rehras) is not mentioned; add if wanted.
Bhagat Trilochan's 'ant kal jo lachhmi simrai' (Gujri, Ang 526) is summarized without the specific rebirths it names; please confirm the summary is fair.
'Sikh teaching prizes honest labor' (kirat karni) is a general statement; please confirm wording.
Original set to null: no single word was central enough to teach.
Editor pass: Trilochan summary brought closer to the text's list (lachhmi, istri, larike, mandar: wealth, wife, sons, mansion) in place of 'a household, a fine house'.
